changes.before: 1.1 [The parenthesisation isometry] The map $(v_1,\dots,v_n)\mapsto v_1\otimes(v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)$ is multilinear from $H^n$ into $H\widehat\otimes H^{\otimes(n-1)}$, so by [F2] applied to the two parenthesisations of the $n$-fold algebraic tensor product it defines a linear map on the algebraic tensor product, and this linear map preserves inner products on elementary tensors by [F1]: $\langle v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n,w_1\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n\rangle=\prod_k\langle v_k,w_k\rangle=\langle v_1,w_1\rangle\langle v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n,w_2\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n\rangle$. Since the elementary tensors span a dense subspace and both sides are complete, [F8] and this isometry identity give a linear isometry $J_n$ on the completed tensor powers, and the image is closed and contains all elementary tensors $v_1\otimes(v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)$, whose span is dense by [F1]; hence $J_n$ is surjective. This proves (b). [F1, F2, F8, algebra]
changes.after: 1.1 [The parenthesisation isometry] For $n=1$, $J_1u=u\otimes1$ is an isometry by [F1], and every tensor in $H\widehat\otimes\mathbb C$ equals $u\otimes1$, so it is surjective. For $n\ge2$, the map $(v_1,\dots,v_n)\mapsto v_1\otimes(v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)$ is multilinear from $H^n$ into $H\widehat\otimes H^{\otimes(n-1)}$, so by [F2] applied to the two parenthesisations of the $n$-fold algebraic tensor product it defines a linear map on the algebraic tensor product, and this linear map preserves inner products on elementary tensors by [F1]: $\langle v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n,w_1\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n\rangle=\prod_k\langle v_k,w_k\rangle=\langle v_1,w_1\rangle\langle v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n,w_2\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n\rangle$. Since the elementary tensors span a dense subspace and both sides are complete, [F8] and this isometry identity give a linear isometry $J_n$ on the completed tensor powers, and the image is closed and contains all elementary tensors $v_1\otimes(v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)$, whose span is dense by [F1]; hence $J_n$ is surjective. This proves (b). [F1, F2, F8, algebra]

changes.before: 1.3 [The zero extension and its symmetry] Regard $\rho$ as an endomorphism of $\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$ and put $\widetilde\rho:=P_\sigma^{(n)}\rho P_\sigma^{(n)}$, an endomorphism of $H^{\otimes n}$ whose restriction to $\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$ is $\rho$ and which vanishes on the orthogonal complement; then $\widetilde\rho\ge0$ and $\operatorname{tr}\widetilde\rho=\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ by [F6] and [F7], so $\widetilde\rho$ is a density operator on $H^{\otimes n}$ with $\widetilde\rho=P_\sigma^{(n)}\widetilde\rho P_\sigma^{(n)}$. Since $U_\pi$ preserves $\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$ and acts on it as the scalar $\operatorname{sgn}_\sigma(\pi)$ by [F4], $U_\pi\widetilde\rho U_\pi^*=\widetilde\rho$ for every $\pi$. [F4, F6, F7, algebra]
changes.after: 1.3 [The zero extension and its symmetry] With $j$ the inclusion of the sector, $\widetilde\rho=j\rho j^*$ restricts to $\rho$ on the sector and vanishes on its orthogonal complement. It is self-adjoint and positive because $\langle\widetilde\rho x,x\rangle=\langle\rho j^*x,j^*x\rangle\ge0$; adjoining an orthonormal basis of the complement to one of the sector gives $\operatorname{tr}\widetilde\rho=\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$, so it is a density operator by [F6]. Since $jj^*=P_\sigma^{(n)}$ and $U_\pi j=\operatorname{sgn}_\sigma(\pi)j$ by [F4], $\widetilde\rho=P_\sigma^{(n)}\widetilde\rho P_\sigma^{(n)}$ and $U_\pi\widetilde\rho U_\pi^*=\widetilde\rho$ for every $\pi$. A zero sector admits no trace-one endomorphism, so no $\rho$ exists in that case. [F4, F6, F7, algebra]

changes.before: 3.1 [Reduction to one slot, the trace law and the reduced operator] Fix $i$ and $\pi$ with $\pi(1)=i$; by steps 1.3 and 2.1 and [F7], $\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho O^{(i)})=\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho U_\pi A_1U_\pi^*)=\operatorname{tr}(U_\pi^*\widetilde\rho U_\pi A_1)=\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho A_1)$, where the middle equality is cyclicity and the last uses $U_\pi^*\widetilde\rho U_\pi=\widetilde\rho$. Therefore $\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho\,\Sigma(O))=\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho O^{(i)})=n\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho A_1)=n\operatorname{tr}((O\otimes I)J_n\widetilde\rho J_n^{-1})=n\operatorname{tr}((\operatorname{Tr}_{H^{\otimes(n-1)}}J_n\widetilde\rho J_n^{-1})O)$ by [F7], [F5] and the explicit form of $A_1$ in step 1.2; with the definition of $\gamma$ this is (d). By [F5] clause (b) applied with $R=J_n\widetilde\rho J_n^{-1}$, which is positive of trace one by step 1.3, the operator $\operatorname{Tr}_{H^{\otimes(n-1)}}J_n\widetilde\rho J_n^{-1}$ is positive of trace one, so its conjugate $\gamma$ is a density operator on $H$. If instead another named slot is retained, the same computation with the corresponding slot operator produces $\gamma'$ with $n\operatorname{tr}((\gamma'-\gamma)O)=0$ for every $O\in\mathcal B(H)$, hence $\gamma'=\gamma$ on testing against the rank-one operators $O=T_{u,v}$, for which $\operatorname{tr}(\gamma T_{u,v})=\langle\gamma u,v\rangle$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]); this proves (e) as well. [F5, F7, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, algebra]
changes.after: 3.1 [Reduction to one slot, the trace law and the reduced operator] By steps 1.3 and 2.1 and [F7], for $\pi(1)=i$ one has $\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho O^{(i)})=\operatorname{tr}(U_\pi^*\widetilde\rho U_\pi A_1)=\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho A_1)$. Set $R_n:=J_n\widetilde\rho J_n^{-1}$, an endomorphism of $H\widehat\otimes H^{\otimes(n-1)}$. Its partial trace $\gamma:=\operatorname{Tr}_{H^{\otimes(n-1)}}R_n$ is an endomorphism of $H$ by [F5]. Step 1.2 and [F5], [F7] give $\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho\Sigma(O))=n\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho A_1)=n\operatorname{tr}(R_n(O\otimes I))=n\operatorname{tr}(\gamma O)$, proving (d). Unitary transport by $J_n$ preserves positivity and trace, so $R_n$ is positive of trace one; [F5] then makes $\gamma$ positive of trace one and hence a density operator on $H$ by [F6]. For the retained slot $i$, use $J_nU_\pi^*$ as the parenthesisation map; its transported state is $J_nU_\pi^*\widetilde\rho U_\pi J_n^{-1}=R_n$ by step 1.3, so its partial trace is the same $\gamma$. More generally the pairing $\operatorname{tr}(\gamma O)=n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho\Sigma(O))$ for every $O$ uniquely determines $\gamma$: testing against $O=T_{u,v}$ gives $\operatorname{tr}(\gamma T_{u,v})=\langle\gamma u,v\rangle$ by [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]] clause (e), which determines every matrix entry. For $n=1$, $J_1u=u\otimes1$, $P_\sigma^{(1)}=I$ and $\Sigma(O)=O$, so this pairing gives $\gamma=\rho$. This proves (e), including the one-particle boundary. [F4, F5, F6, F7, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, algebra]
